key_terms.meaning: The line that joins a point to the geographic north pole; bearings measured from it are true bearings and do not change with time.
The direction in which a freely suspended compass needle settles at a place; it shifts slowly from year to year.
Any convenient fixed line chosen as the reference north when no true or magnetic north is needed, common in small local surveys.
The angle a line makes with a chosen meridian, measured clockwise from 0° to 360° in the whole-circle system.
A direction measured clockwise from north, the same as a whole circle bearing; true azimuth is measured from true north.
The bearing of a line taken in the direction of progress along the traverse, from the station occupied to the station ahead.
The bearing of the same line taken in the reverse direction; it differs from the fore bearing by exactly 180°.
The angle between the true meridian and the magnetic meridian at a place, east or west of true north; true bearing = magnetic bearing ± declination.
A line drawn on a map through all places having the same magnetic declination.
An isogonic line along which the magnetic declination is zero, so true and magnetic north coincide.
The angle between the prolongation of the previous line and the next line; it is right or left and is less than 180°.
The angle between two adjacent traverse lines measured inside the closed figure; the sum for a closed polygon of n sides is (2n − 4) × 90°.
The deflection of a magnetic needle from the magnetic meridian caused by nearby iron objects, steel tapes, rails or current-carrying wires.
A drawing board mounted on a tripod with a sighting alidade and a magnetic compass, used to plot the map directly in the field.
A plane table method in which rays are drawn from one set-up station to every object and distances are scaled along those rays.
A plane table method in which the object is fixed by the crossing of rays drawn from two or more set-up stations, with no distance measured.
The north–south component of a traverse line: l cos θ, with l the length and θ the whole circle bearing; positive north, negative south.
The east–west component of a traverse line: l sin θ, with l the length and θ the whole circle bearing; positive east, negative west.
The gap between the starting station and the computed end of a closed traverse, found from e = √((ΣL)² + (ΣD)²).
A traverse adjustment in which the total error in latitude and departure is spread in proportion to the length of each line.

takeaways: A bearing is meaningless until you say which north it was measured from, so always state true, magnetic, grid or arbitrary.
The same direction can be written as a whole-circle bearing, a reduced bearing, a back bearing or an interior angle; converting correctly is a skill worth drilling.
Magnetic declination changes with place and time, so a compass bearing must carry its date and location to be useful.
Local attraction is detected by comparing fore and back bearings; the stations that agree are free of it and become the reference.
Plane table surveying trades precision for speed: it plots directions directly but cannot measure distances you did not tape.
Latitude and departure turn a traverse into simple vector sums, which is why every adjustment rule works on these two columns.
A closed traverse almost never closes by itself; the closing error is evidence of small systematic and random errors, not of one blunder.
Bowditch's rule suits compass traverses, where bearings are as uncertain as lengths; the transit rule suits theodolite traverses where angles are better than lengths.
The coordinate or shoelace method gives the area of any closed polygon from its corner coordinates, with no scaling or planimeter.
Sign conventions for latitude and departure must be fixed before any table is made, or the whole adjustment goes wrong.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually judged on correct conversion between whole-circle and reduced bearings, a clean local-attraction correction table, a full latitude–departure table with Bowditch adjustment, and area by coordinates shown in a closed tabular form.

bank.q: Define true meridian, magnetic meridian, grid meridian and arbitrary meridian. Explain why a bearing written in a field book is incomplete unless the meridian is also named.
outline: Definition of each meridian with a one-line sketch
True north is fixed by the pole star or by astronomical observation; magnetic north is what the needle shows
Grid north is the direction of the map grid lines, close to true north but not equal
Arbitrary meridian chosen for a local survey only
A bearing is an angle from a stated reference, so the same line has four different numerical values
answer: Meridian. A meridian is the reference line through a station from which the direction of a survey line is measured. A bearing is the angle between the line and that meridian.

True meridian. The line through the station and the geographic north and south poles. It is fixed by astronomical observation (or from GNSS) and does not change with time, so true bearings are permanent and are used for property boundaries and maps.

Magnetic meridian. The direction in which a freely suspended, balanced magnetic needle comes to rest at the station. It points to magnetic north, which differs from true north by the magnetic declination, and it drifts slowly year by year.

Grid meridian. A line parallel to the central meridian of the map projection (the grid lines running north on the sheet). It is the north of a projected coordinate system; away from the central meridian it differs slightly from true north.

Arbitrary meridian. Any convenient fixed line, such as the line from a station to a temple spire or a corner of a building, used as north in a small local survey. It is easy to set up again but means nothing outside that survey.

answer.text: Why a bearing needs its meridian. One line has a different bearing from each meridian. Example: a line with magnetic bearing 40°00′ where the declination is 5°30′ east has a true bearing of 45°30′; on a sheet whose grid north is 0°45′ west of true north at that place, its grid bearing is 46°15′.

head: Meridian
Bearing of the same line
rows: Arbitrary (line to a spire at true 12°00′)

answer: Consequence. A field book entry such as "AB 40°00′" is incomplete: the same number set out from true north instead of magnetic north turns the line by 5°30′, which moves its far end by 100 × tan 5°30′ = 9.6 m at 100 m. The book must say which north (and, for magnetic, the date and place).

True meridians converge. True meridians meet at the poles, so they are not parallel. Two stations 1 km apart east–west at latitude 13° lie 1/(111.32 cos 13°) = 0.00922° of longitude apart, and their true meridians differ in direction by 0.00922° × sin 13° = 0.00207°, about 7.5″. This is negligible in a compass survey but matters in long theodolite and GNSS work, which is why grid meridians, all parallel, are used for coordinates.

Which meridian in practice. Magnetic for compass surveys, because the needle gives it at once; true for property boundaries, maps and long routes, because it does not change; grid for coordinate work with total stations and GNSS on a projected sheet; arbitrary for a small site plan that will never be joined to a map.
Check. Each bearing in the table differs from the magnetic value only by the angle between its meridian and magnetic north (5°30′, 6°15′ and −6°30′), so all four describe the same ground line.

bank.q: Explain magnetic declination and isogonic lines. How is a magnetic bearing converted to a true bearing when the declination is 3°15′ east?
outline: Declination is the angle between true and magnetic meridians at a place
East declination: true bearing = magnetic bearing + declination
West declination: true bearing = magnetic bearing − declination
Isogonic lines join places of equal declination; the agonic line is the zero-declination line
Worked conversion with 3°15′ east, giving a numerical answer
Declination changes with time, so the year of observation must be stated
answer: Declination. Magnetic declination is the horizontal angle between the true meridian and the magnetic meridian at a place. It is east when magnetic north lies east of true north, and west when it lies west.

Why it varies. The earth's magnetic field is not aligned with its axis and changes slowly, so declination differs from place to place and changes with time (secular variation), with small daily changes as well. A declination is therefore quoted with its place and year.

Isogonic and agonic lines. An isogonic line joins places with the same declination; an agonic line joins places with zero declination, where the needle points to true north. Maps of these lines let a surveyor read the declination for a site.

answer.text: Rule. With east declination the needle points east of true north, so the magnetic bearing of every line is smaller than its true bearing:
answer.pre:
east declination:  true bearing = magnetic bearing + declination
west declination:  true bearing = magnetic bearing − declination

answer.text: Worked conversion, declination 3°15′ east.

answer: The reverse. A true bearing of 115°45′ set out with a compass at the same place is laid off as 115°45′ − 3°15′ = 112°30′ magnetic.

Change with time. If a map gives 3°15′ E in 2016 with an annual change of 2′ westward, then in 2026 the declination is 3°15′ − 10 × 2′ = 2°55′ E, and the 112°30′ line would read 115°45′ − 2°55′ = 112°50′ on a compass that year.

Finding the declination at a site. (1) Read it from an isogonic chart or a geomagnetic model for the place and date. (2) Observe the true bearing of a line by the sun or Polaris and read the same line with the compass. If the true bearing of PQ is 72°09′ and the compass reads 69°05′, the declination is 72°09′ − 69°05′ = 3°04′, east because the true bearing is the larger.

answer.text: West declination, for contrast. With 1°20′ W the true bearing is smaller than the magnetic bearing:

answer: Variations to allow for. Secular variation (over years, the largest), annual variation (a few minutes over the year), diurnal variation (a few minutes over the day) and irregular changes during magnetic storms. A compass survey repeated years later must be brought to the declination of the new date before old and new bearings are compared, or the same boundary will appear to have turned.
Check. Reverse each answer: 115°45′ − 3°15′ = 112°30′ and 1°15′ + 360° − 3°15′ = 358°00′, the magnetic bearings given.

bank.q: List the four methods of plane table surveying and state one situation where each is preferred.
outline: Radiation: small area surveyed from a single station
Intersection or triangulation: distant or inaccessible objects, no chaining possible
Traversing: long narrow strips such as roads and canals
Resection: the table is set up at an unknown point and located by sights to known points
One practical situation for each method
answer: Common start. In every method the table is set up, levelled, centred over the station with the plumbing fork, and oriented (by trough compass or by backsighting a plotted line) before rays are drawn.

Radiation. From one station O, rays are drawn with the alidade to every object and the distance to each is taped and scaled along its ray. Preferred for a small open area visible from one point, such as a playground or a building site with all corners within one tape length or two.

Intersection (graphic triangulation). From the two ends of a measured base line, rays are drawn to each object; the crossing of the rays fixes it and no distance to the object is measured. Preferred for inaccessible or distant points: a tree across a river, the far bank of a stream, a spire.

Traversing. The table is moved from station to station along the route; at each station it is oriented by backsighting the previous station, the next line is drawn and its length taped. Preferred for long narrow strips: a road, a canal, a stream course.

Resection. The table stands at a point not yet plotted, and its position on the sheet is found by sighting points already plotted (two-point or three-point problem). Preferred when the table must be set up at a convenient spot that was not occupied before, for example to pick up detail hidden from the existing stations.

answer.text: Summary.

answer: Two-point and three-point problems. In resection the three-point problem uses three well-spaced plotted points sighted from the new station; the tracing-paper method or Lehmann's trial method (shrinking the triangle of error) fixes the station. The two-point problem uses only two plotted points and an auxiliary station, so it takes longer and is used only when a third point is not visible.

answer.text: Scale and orientation in numbers. At 1:500 a taped distance of 42.5 m is drawn 42.5/500 = 0.085 m = 8.5 cm along the ray. An orientation error of 1° moves a point 50 m away sideways by 50 × tan 1° = 0.87 m on the ground, which is 1.75 mm on the sheet, seven times the 0.25 mm plotting accuracy. This is why orientation by backsighting is preferred to the trough compass.

answer: Check. Intersection needs a good angle of cut (roughly 30° to 150° between the rays); a cut that is too narrow makes the crossing point uncertain along the rays.

bank.q: Explain latitude and departure of a traverse line. Derive the formulas and state the sign convention for each quadrant.
outline: Latitude is the component along the north–south axis, departure along the east–west axis
From the right triangle: latitude = l cos θ and departure = l sin θ, with θ the whole circle bearing (or the reduced bearing with signs from the quadrant letters)
Sign convention: north positive, south negative for latitude; east positive, west negative for departure
Table of signs for NE, SE, SW and NW quadrants
Check: √(L² + D²) must return the line length
answer: Definitions. The latitude of a line is its projection on the north–south axis; the departure is its projection on the east–west axis. Together they are the northing and easting changes from one end of the line to the other.

Derivation. Draw the line AB of length l with whole circle bearing θ from north. Drop a perpendicular from B to the north line through A. The right triangle has hypotenuse l and angle θ at A, so the side along north is l cos θ and the side along east is l sin θ.

answer.text: Formulas.
answer.pre:
latitude  L = l cos θ    (+ north, − south)
departure D = l sin θ    (+ east,  − west)
with a reduced bearing α:  L = ± l cos α,  D = ± l sin α, signs from the letters

answer.text: Signs by quadrant.
Worked lines.

answer: Use. Because latitudes and departures are signed components, they add like vectors: their sums give the coordinate changes, and in a closed traverse both sums must be zero.

Why cos for latitude. The bearing is measured from north, so the side next to the angle (the adjacent side) lies along north: latitude uses cos θ and departure, the opposite side, uses sin θ. If the angle were measured from east, the two would swap.

answer.text: Worked line with a reduced bearing. A line 150 m long at S 35°20′ E lies in the SE quadrant: latitude negative, departure positive.
Going back from components to the line. The length is √(L² + D²) and the reduced bearing is tan α = |D|/|L|, with the quadrant read from the signs.
From components to coordinates. The coordinates of the far end are those of the near end plus the latitude (northing) and departure (easting). With A at (1000 E, 1000 N):

answer: Closed traverse sums. For the four worked lines, ΣL = 141.42 − 127.28 − 138.56 + 124.19 = −0.23 m and ΣD = 141.42 + 127.28 − 80.00 − 188.82 = −0.12 m. Both should be zero; the small remainders are the closing error, which is adjusted before plotting.

bank.q: Describe the checks used to test a compass traverse before adjustment.
outline: Difference between fore bearing and back bearing should be 180°; difference from 180° indicates local attraction or a reading blunder
Sum of interior angles should equal (2n − 4) × 90° for a closed polygon
Sum of deflection angles should be 360°
Sum of latitudes and sum of departures of a closed traverse should each be zero
Any large single mismatch points to a recording blunder rather than to local attraction
answer: Why check before adjusting. Adjustment spreads small errors; it must never hide a blunder or local attraction. Four checks are made on the field data first.

1. Fore and back bearings. For every line, FB − BB = ±180°. A line that passes proves both its stations free from local attraction. Example: AB 46°00′ and BA 226°00′ differ by 180°00′, so A and B are free; CD 220°30′ and DC 40°00′ differ by 180°30′, so C or D is affected.

answer.text: 2. Sum of interior angles. For a closed polygon of n sides the interior angles sum to (2n − 4) × 90°. Local attraction does not affect an included angle (both bearings at a station are turned equally), so this check tests reading and booking.

answer: 3. Sum of deflection angles. For a closed traverse the algebraic sum of the deflection angles (right positive, left negative) is 360°.

answer.text: 4. Sums of latitudes and departures. For a closed traverse ΣL = 0 and ΣD = 0. The closing error e = √(ΣL² + ΣD²) and the relative precision P/e must meet the limit.

answer: Reading the checks. Many small mismatches suggest ordinary random error; one large mismatch suggests a blunder. A closing error that lies parallel to one line suggests a wrong length in that line; a bearing blunder moves the end at right angles to the line.

5. Closing on known points. When the traverse runs between two stations whose coordinates are known, ΣL must equal Nend − Nstart and ΣD must equal Eend − Estart. Example: from (500.00 E, 800.00 N) to (742.30 E, 655.10 N), the sums should be ΣL = −144.90 m and ΣD = +242.30 m.

6. Field checks on lengths and directions. Measure each line in both directions (the two lengths should agree to about 1 in 500 for chained lines); sight a distant prominent object, such as a chimney, from several stations and see that its bearings plot to one point; take a tie line across the figure between two stations and compare its measured length with the length computed from the traverse.

Acceptance. A compass traverse is commonly accepted at a relative precision of about 1 in 300 to 1 in 600. The example closes at 1 in 2950, so it passes comfortably and can go on to adjustment by Bowditch's rule.
Check. The angle-sum correction −7′30″ × 4 = −30′ removes the +30′ exactly.

bank.q: The observed bearings of a closed compass traverse ABCD are: AB 61°15′, BA 239°30′, BC 140°00′, CB 320°45′, CD 230°30′, DC 50°30′, DA 320°15′, AD 141°15′. Find the stations affected by local attraction, the correction at each, the corrected bearings and the included angles.
outline: Tabulate stations, line, observed fore bearing and back bearing
Find the line whose fore and back bearings differ by exactly 180°; its two stations are free from local attraction
Compute the local attraction at each other station as the difference between the observed and the correct bearing
Carry the correction forward station by station, correcting the back bearing first and then the fore bearing
Convert corrected bearings to interior or included angles with a sketch
Verify the angle sum against (2n − 4) × 90°
answer: Method. A station is free of local attraction if a line through it has fore and back bearings differing by exactly 180°. Start from such a line, correct the stations one after another, and check that the corrections close.

answer.text: Step 1: test every line.

answer: Step 2: from the free stations. C and D are free, so CD = 230°30′, DC = 50°30′, CB = 320°45′ and DA = 320°15′ are correct as observed.

answer.text: Step 3: station A. Correct AD = DA − 180° = 320°15′ − 180° = 140°15′. Observed AD = 141°15′, so A reads 1°00′ too much: correction at A = −1°00′. Corrected AB = 61°15′ − 1°00′ = 60°15′.
Step 4: station B. Correct BA = AB + 180° = 60°15′ + 180° = 240°15′. Observed BA = 239°30′, so correction at B = +0°45′. Corrected BC = 140°00′ + 0°45′ = 140°45′.

answer: Step 5: close the loop. Correct CB from the corrected BC = 140°45′ + 180° = 320°45′, equal to the observed CB at the free station C. The corrections are consistent.

answer.text: Corrected bearings.
Included angles. At each station, the angle between the two lines (taken inside the figure). Local attraction cancels, so observed and corrected bearings give the same angles.

answer: Which way the needle was pulled. Bearings are read clockwise from the needle. At A the observed bearings are 1°00′ too large, so the north end of the needle was pulled 1°00′ west (anticlockwise) by some nearby iron; at B they are 0°45′ too small, so the needle was pulled 0°45′ east. Every bearing read at a station carries the same error, which is why one correction per station is enough.

answer.text: Second method: run the bearings from the included angles. Start from the free line CD and carry the bearings round with the interior angles; the result must return to CD.
Corrected bearings in reduced form.

answer: Precautions in the field. Keep the chain, arrows, steel tapes, keys and phones away from the compass; avoid stations near rails, steel poles, buried pipes and power lines; read both the fore and back bearing of every line, since only that pair reveals local attraction. Local attraction does not affect the included angles, so the angle sum check (360° here) tests reading and booking but cannot detect it.

Result. Stations A and B are affected by local attraction; the correction is −1°00′ at A and +0°45′ at B, and C and D need none. If no line had fore and back bearings exactly 180° apart, the included angles would be computed first, checked against 360°, and the bearings carried round from the line with the smallest discrepancy.
Check. Using observed bearings at A: 141°15′ − 61°15′ = 80°00′, the same as the corrected value, confirming that local attraction leaves the included angle unchanged.

bank.q: A closed traverse ABCD has AB = 200 m, N 45° E; BC = 180 m, S 45° E; CD = 160 m, S 30° W; DA = 226 m, N 56°40′ W. Prepare the latitude and departure table, find the closing error and its bearing, and adjust the traverse by Bowditch's rule. Give the coordinates of B, C and D with A at (1000 E, 1000 N).
outline: Latitude ± l cos α and departure ± l sin α from each reduced bearing α, signs from the quadrant letters
Sum the latitudes and the departures; both should in principle be zero
Closing error e = √((ΣL)² + (ΣD)²) and its bearing from tan θ = ΣD / ΣL
Bowditch correction in latitude of a line = total error in latitude × (line length ÷ perimeter), with opposite sign
Same formula for departure; corrected values should sum to zero
Show the final corrected coordinates of every station

answer.text: Latitude and departure table. L = ± l cos α, D = ± l sin α, with α the reduced bearing and the signs from the letters.
Components, line by line.
Closing error.
Bowditch corrections. CL = −ΣL × l/P = +0.23 × l/766; CD = −ΣD × l/P = +0.12 × l/766.
Corrections, line by line. Each correction has the sign opposite to the sum.

answer: Rounding. The departure corrections to 4 decimals are 0.0313, 0.0282, 0.0251 and 0.0354 m; rounded to millimetres they sum to 0.119 m, so the largest (DA) is rounded up to 0.036 m to make the sum exactly 0.120 m.

answer.text: Coordinates.
Coordinates, step by step.
How far each station moves. The unadjusted traverse ends at A′, 0.259 m from A towards S 27°33′ W. Bowditch moves each station towards N 27°33′ E by e × (distance along the traverse)/P:
What the adjustment did to the lines. Bowditch changes the lengths and bearings slightly:

answer: Is the result acceptable? A compass traverse is commonly accepted at 1 in 300 to 1 in 600; this one closes at 1 in 2950, so adjustment is justified. The stations are then plotted from their coordinates, each from the origin, so a plotting slip at one station is not carried to the next.
Check. The adjusted latitudes and departures each sum to 0.000, and walking the coordinates round from A returns to (1000.000, 1000.000).

bank.q: The corners of an irregular plot, in order, are A (100, 100), B (180, 120), C (200, 200), D (140, 250) and E (80, 190), eastings and northings in metres. Compute its area by the coordinate method, state the formula used, and give the area in hectares.
outline: Arrange the corners in order around the boundary, clockwise or anticlockwise but consistent
Twice the area = Σ E<sub>i</sub>(N<sub>i+1</sub> − N<sub>i−1</sub>), or Σ(E<sub>i</sub>N<sub>i+1</sub> − E<sub>i+1</sub>N<sub>i</sub>), with wrap-around
Area = half the magnitude of the sum, in square metres
Convert to hectares by dividing by 10 000
Check with the second form of the formula

answer.text: Formula. For corners numbered in order round the boundary,
answer.pre: 2A = Σ E<sub>i</sub> (N<sub>i+1</sub> − N<sub>i−1</sub>)        (wrap round: after E comes A, before A comes E)

answer.text: Table.

answer: Area. 2A = 23 600 m², so A = 11 800 m² = 11 800/10 000 = 1.18 ha. The sum is positive because the corners run anticlockwise.

answer.text: Check by the second form.

answer: Points to watch. Keep the corners in boundary order (A, C, B, D, E would cross itself and give a wrong number); use the wrap-around rows; halve the sum; take the magnitude if the sum is negative.

answer.text: Third check: trapezoids. Each side with the north axis forms a trapezoid of area ½ (Ei + Ei+1)(Ni+1 − Ni); added round the boundary they give the area.
Shifting the origin to save arithmetic. Subtracting 80 from every easting and 100 from every northing moves the plot but not its area: E′ = 20, 100, 120, 60, 0 and N′ = 0, 20, 100, 150, 90.

answer: When the corners come from a traverse. Use the adjusted coordinates, not the raw ones, so that the polygon closes; the double meridian distance method on the adjusted latitudes and departures gives the same area.
Units. 1 ha = 10 000 m², so 11 800 m² = 1.18 ha; in acres (1 acre = 4046.86 m²) it is 11 800/4046.86 = 2.92 acres.
Check. The plot fits inside the rectangle 80 to 200 m east and 100 to 250 m north, of area 120 × 150 = 18 000 m²; 11 800 m² is about two thirds of it, which matches the shape.

bank.q: Explain the radiation, intersection and traversing methods of plane table surveying with a sketch of each, and state the field checks used.
outline: Radiation: single station, rays to all objects, distances scaled; suit small areas
Intersection: two or more stations, rays drawn from each, object at the crossing; suit distant objects
Traversing: table shifted along the route, each leg plotted; suit roads and canals
Checks: two-point and three-point problem for orientation, closing the traverse on the starting station
Limitations: weather, weight of the board, scale distortion on large areas

answer.text: Sketches. Radiation, intersection and traversing.

answer: Setting up. In all three, level the board, centre it over the station with the plumbing fork, and orient it (trough compass, or backsight along a plotted line) before drawing rays.

Radiation. Set up at O, near the middle of the area, and mark o on the sheet. Sight each object with the alidade pivoted on o, draw a ray, tape the distance and scale it along the ray. Example: a corner 36.0 m away at 1:500 is plotted 36.0/500 = 7.2 cm from o. Suits a small area seen from one station.

Intersection. Measure a base line AB and plot it as ab. Set up at A, orient along AB, and draw rays to every object; move to B, orient by backsighting A, and draw rays to the same objects. Each crossing fixes an object without taping to it. Example: a 60 m base at 1:500 is 12 cm on the sheet. Suits inaccessible points; keep the angle of cut between about 30° and 150°.

Traversing. Set up at A, orient, draw the ray to B and plot the taped length; move to B, orient by backsighting A, draw the ray to C, and so on. Detail is picked up from each station by radiation or intersection. Suits roads and canals.

Field checks. Draw a check ray to a third point from each station (it should pass through the plotted point); in intersection, fix one point from three stations, which should meet at one point; in traversing, close on the starting station or on a known point, and distribute any small closing error graphically in proportion to distance; re-check orientation by sighting a distant plotted point before leaving each station.
Limitations. The board is heavy and awkward in wind and rain, the sheet is exposed, and the accuracy is graphic: about 0.25 mm on paper, which is 0.125 m on the ground at 1:500.

Equipment. Drawing board on a tripod, alidade (plain or telescopic) with a fiducial edge, plumbing fork with plumb bob, spirit level, trough compass, drawing sheet fixed to the board, and a tape for distances.

Orientation and centring in numbers. An orientation error of 1° moves a point 50 m away by 50 × tan 1° = 0.87 m, which is 1.75 mm at 1:500, so backsighting is preferred to the trough compass. A centring error e on the ground shifts the plotted point by e/500 at 1:500; keeping that under 0.25 mm needs e under 0.25 mm × 500 = 0.125 m, which the plumbing fork easily gives.

answer.text: Intersection worked. Base AB = 60 m. At A the ray to a tree T makes 62° with AB; at B it makes 55° with BA. The angle at T is 180° − 62° − 55° = 63°, a good cut. The sine rule gives the distances the rays should show when scaled:

answer: Traversing: closing on the sheet. If a plane table traverse of 60 cm total length on the sheet closes with a 4.0 mm gap, each station is moved parallel to the gap by 4.0 mm × (distance along the traverse)/60 cm; a station 36 cm along moves 4.0 × 36/60 = 2.4 mm, and the last station moves the full 4.0 mm onto the start.

Choosing among them. On one survey they are often combined: a traverse gives the frame of stations, radiation picks up the nearby detail from each, and intersection fixes the points that cannot be reached.
Check. At 1:500, 1 cm on paper is 5 m on the ground: 7.2 cm × 5 = 36.0 m, matching the taped distance in the radiation example.

bank.q: A line has a whole-circle bearing of 236°40′. Write its reduced bearing, its back bearing in both systems, and the deflection angle if the next line has a whole-circle bearing of 300°.
outline: Reduced bearing = 236°40′ − 180° = 56°40′ in the SW quadrant, written S 56°40′ W
Back bearing is 236°40′ − 180° = 56°40′ whole circle, that is N 56°40′ E
Deflection angle = 300° − 236°40′ = 63°20′ to the right
Show the conversion rules for all four quadrants clearly
State that whole-circle bearings run 0° to 360° clockwise
answer: Quadrant. 236°40′ lies between 180° and 270°, so the line points south-west.

answer.text: Reduced bearing.
Back bearing. FB is more than 180°, so subtract 180°.
Deflection angle. The deflection is the angle from the prolongation of the first line to the next line; it equals the difference of the forward bearings.
Rules for all quadrants.
Sketch.

answer: Convention. Whole circle bearings run from 0° to 360° clockwise from north; a reduced bearing is always 90° or less and names the meridian end (N or S) first.

Back bearing in both systems. In the whole circle system the back bearing differs by exactly 180°: 56°40′. In the reduced system the angle stays 56°40′ and only the letters swap: S 56°40′ W becomes N 56°40′ E.
The next line. WCB 300° lies between 270° and 360°, so its reduced bearing is N (360° − 300°) W = N 60°00′ W, and its back bearing is 120°00′ = S 60°00′ E.

answer.text: The same deflection from reduced bearings. Walk round from the direction of the first line, carried on past its end (S 56°40′ W, that is 236°40′), clockwise to the next line (N 60°00′ W, that is 300°):

answer: Why the sign matters. A right (clockwise) deflection is booked positive and a left one negative; in a closed traverse the algebraic sum of all deflections must be 360°, so a wrong side shows at once in that check.

answer.text: Components of a 50 m line on this bearing. Both are negative in the SW quadrant.

answer: Check. The included angle between the back bearing of the first line (56°40′) and the next line (300°) is 300° − 56°40′ = 243°20′ on one side, 116°40′ on the other; 180° − 116°40′ = 63°20′, the deflection found.

bank.q: Compare plane table surveying with compass traversing for a small topographic survey. Under what field conditions would you choose each?
outline: Plane table plots in the field, so no field book and no later plotting errors
Compass traverse records angles and distances; plotting happens later in the office with instruments
Plane table is fast for small-scale detail work but awkward on steep or windy ground
Compass work is affected by local attraction; plane table alidade is not magnetic unless a compass box is used
Accuracy: compass traverse with a tape gives better distances; plane table orientation errors accumulate
Choose plane table for rapid small-area mapping, compass for a long traverse needing recorded data
answer: What each records. The plane table draws the map in the field: directions are rays on the sheet and distances are scaled on them. The compass traverse records bearings and lengths in a field book, and the plan is plotted (or the coordinates computed) later.

answer.text: Comparison.
Size of the errors. A 30′ error in a compass bearing moves the end of a 100 m line sideways by 100 × tan 0°30′; a plotting error of 0.25 mm at 1:1000 is 0.25 m on the ground.

answer: When to choose the plane table. A small, open, fairly flat area that needs a plan with plenty of detail quickly (a campus block, a village site at 1:500 or 1:1000), in fair weather, where the absence of a numerical record does not matter.

When to choose the compass traverse. A long or wooded route (a forest track, a stream), rough ground or bad weather, or where the measurements must be kept and computed later; avoid it near railways, steel structures and power lines.
Combining them. A compass traverse can give the frame, and the plane table can fill in detail from its stations.

Errors peculiar to each. Plane table: orientation, centring, the alidade edge not passing through the station point, paper shrinkage and the instability of the board. Compass traverse: local attraction, a sluggish or bent needle, reading the ring to only 15′ or 30′, change of declination during the work, and plotting errors when the book is drawn up.

answer.text: A small topographic survey, in numbers. A site of about 200 m × 150 m mapped at 1:500 with some 60 detail points:
answer.pre:
plane table: plotting accuracy 0.25 mm × 500 = 0.125 m
compass: 30′ error at 150 m = 150 × tan 0°30′ = 1.31 m sideways
compass traverse of 700 m at 1 in 300 to 1 in 600: closing error 2.33 m to 1.17 m

answer.text: Choosing by field conditions.

head: Condition
Choose
Why
rows: plan drawn while the ground is in view
light, needs only the next station in sight
Near steel, rails or power lines
the sheet cannot be kept dry and still
Data must be kept and recomputed
the field book is a numerical record

answer: Recommendation for the example site. A 200 m × 150 m open block with 60 detail points is a plane table job: two or three stations by radiation and intersection, the plan finished on site in about a day, and every point within 0.125 m. If the block were wooded or the work had to continue in the rains, a compass traverse round it with offsets to the detail would be chosen instead, accepting metre-level error.

Check. On a 100 m line, the compass error (0.87 m) is larger than the plane-table plotting error at 1:1000 (0.25 m), so for short-range detail the plane table is the more precise of the two; over long routes the traverse keeps its edge because its errors can be checked and adjusted.

bank.q: Compare Bowditch's rule and the transit rule for adjusting a closed traverse, using the traverse AB 200 m at 45°, BC 180 m at 135°, CD 160 m at 210°, DA 226 m at 303°20′ (ΣL = −0.23 m, ΣD = −0.12 m). State which rule suits which instrument and why.
outline: Bowditch: corrections proportional to line length, assumes angular and linear errors are equally likely
Transit rule: corrections proportional to the magnitude of latitude or departure, assumes angular work is more precise
Bowditch suits compass traverses where bearings and lengths are of similar reliability
Transit rule suits theodolite traverses with taped or EDM lengths
Both remove the closing error but redistribute it differently; large errors should not be blindly adjusted
Guard against using adjustment to hide a blunder: first check the angle sum and the fore–back bearing difference
answer: The rules. Bowditch (compass) rule: correction to a latitude or departure = −(total error) × l/P, proportional to line length. Transit rule: correction to a latitude = −ΣL × |L|/Σ|L|, and to a departure = −ΣD × |D|/Σ|D|, proportional to the size of the component.

The assumptions. Bowditch assumes angular and linear errors produce equal shifts, so a line's share depends only on its length. The transit rule assumes angles are much more precise than lengths, so each component is corrected by its own size and the bearings change very little.

answer.text: Working for one line (CD).
Transit rule, line by line.

answer: Reading the table. Both rules remove the whole error (the sums are +0.230 and +0.120). They differ line by line: the transit rule gives CD more latitude correction (its latitude is large) and less departure correction (its departure is small), while Bowditch treats CD only by its length.

answer.text: Adjusted coordinates by each rule (A at 1000 E, 1000 N):

answer: Effect on the bearings. CD was observed at 210°00′00″. After Bowditch it is 210°00′06″; after the transit rule it is 210°00′21″, because CD received a large latitude correction and a small departure correction. For a compass traverse read to 30′ either change is far below the reading accuracy.

Which rule for which instrument. A compass traverse, with bearings to 30′ and taped lengths, has angular and linear errors of similar effect: Bowditch. A theodolite or total station traverse, with angles to seconds and lengths less precise in proportion, suits the transit rule. Least squares, using weights, is the rigorous method for either.
Before any rule. Check the angle sum and the fore and back bearings first; a closing error far beyond the expected precision points to a blunder, which no rule should spread.

A known weakness of the transit rule. Its corrections depend on the direction of the north axis: turn the same traverse through 45° and the latitudes and departures change, so the adjustment changes. Bowditch's rule depends only on lengths and gives the same result whatever the orientation.

answer.text: Summary of the choice.

Assumes
Suits
Bearings after adjustment
rows: angular and linear errors of equal effect
compass and tape, plane table traverses
change a little on every line
theodolite or total station with tape
change least where one component dominates

bank.q: A student's compass traverse ABCD (AB 200 m at 45°, BC 180 m at 135°, CD 160 m at 210°, DA 226 m at 303°20′, all after local-attraction corrections) gives ΣL = +8.43 m and ΣD = +4.88 m. Explain the possible sources of error and the checks that localise the fault, and find the most likely fault here.
outline: Classify errors into instrumental, personal and natural
Instrumental: needle not straight, pivot friction, sluggish needle, bent sight vanes
Personal: reading the circle carelessly, wrong booking, wrong sign while entering bearings
Natural: local attraction from nearby iron, cables, rails; magnetic declination not applied
Checks: fore and back bearing difference, interior angle sum, closing error direction
A single large discrepancy points to a blunder; many small ones point to systematic error
answer: Size of the misclosure. e = √(8.43² + 4.88²) = √(71.06 + 23.81) = √94.88 = 9.74 m in a perimeter of 766 m: 1 in 79. That is far too large for random error; something is wrong.

answer.text: Possible sources.

head: Kind
Examples
rows: bent needle or sight vanes, blunt pivot, sluggish needle, tape of wrong length
reading the ring carelessly, booking 150 for 160 or a bearing in the wrong column, counting tape lengths wrongly
local attraction not detected, magnetic changes during the day

answer: Checks that localise a fault. (1) Fore and back bearings of each line (after correction they should differ by 180°). (2) The included-angle sum against (2n − 4) × 90°. (3) The direction of the closing error: a wrong length moves the end parallel to the faulty line; a wrong bearing moves it at right angles to the line, by about l × the angle error.

answer.text: Direction of this error.
answer.pre:
tan θ = 4.88/8.43 = 0.579, θ = 30°04′; both sums positive → bearing 30°04′ (NE)
line CD runs at 210°, its reverse at 30°: the error is parallel to CD

answer.text: Testing the guess. If CD was taped as 150 m instead of 160 m, the missing 10 m along 210° would add the reverse of its components to the sums:

answer: Conclusion. The fault is a 10 m blunder in the length of CD (one tape length of 10 m, or 150 booked for 160). Re-measure CD; with 160 m the traverse closes to 0.26 m (1 in 2950), and only then adjust it by Bowditch.

answer.text: The sums recomputed with CD = 150 m.

The other candidate rejected. A bearing blunder moves the end at right angles to the faulty line. The only line whose perpendicular is near 30° is DA (303°20′ − 270° = 33°20′). To produce 9.74 m, DA would need a bearing error of 9.74/226 rad:
answer.pre:
9.74/226 = 0.0431 rad = 2°28′, giving an error at 33°20′
observed error direction 30°04′: 3°16′ away, and 2°28′ is not a likely misreading
CD 10 m short: error at 30°00′, size 10.00 m, sums agree to 0.01 m

answer: The angle check agrees. The included angles from the corrected bearings sum to 360°, so the bearings are consistent with each other; that points the search at a length rather than a bearing.

Expected size of honest error. At 1 in 300 to 1 in 600, a 766 m compass traverse should close within 766/300 = 2.55 m to 766/600 = 1.28 m. The student's 9.74 m is four to eight times that, so it cannot be spread by Bowditch; it must be found.
After re-measurement. With CD = 160 m the traverse closes to 0.259 m and Bowditch's rule gives B (1141.451, 1141.480), C (1268.759, 1014.254) and D (1188.784, 875.742) with A at (1000, 1000).

Prevention. Count tape lengths with the ten arrows and check the count at the end of every line; read the length back aloud before booking; and measure each line forward and back, which would have shown 150 m one way and 160 m the other.
Check. After correcting CD the sums return to ΣL = −0.23 m and ΣD = −0.12 m, the values of an ordinary small misclosure.

glossary.def: A reference direction line from the station to some north, from which bearings are measured clockwise.
A bearing measured clockwise from north through the full 0° to 360° range, also called the azimuth.
A bearing written as an acute angle from the nearer end of the north–south line, with a quadrant letter such as N 30° E.
A small magnetised steel needle pivoted at its centre that aligns itself with the local magnetic field.
A survey compass with a prism eyepiece that lets the observer read the graduated ring while sighting the object.
A plain compass with a graduated ring and two sight vanes, read by eye from above the needle.
The north direction defined by the vertical grid lines of a map projection, used for grid bearings.
The angle at a traverse station between the two lines meeting there, measured either inside or outside the figure.
A series of connected survey lines whose lengths and directions are measured to fix the positions of successive stations.
A traverse that returns to its starting station (a loop) or ends on another station of known position (a link traverse), so its closure can be checked.
A traverse that starts at a known point and ends at an unknown one, so no closure check is possible.
The total length of all lines of the traverse, used as the denominator in Bowditch's distribution.
A straight-edge ruler with a sight, used on the plane table to draw rays in the sighted direction.
Setting the plane table so that lines already drawn on the sheet point in the same true directions as on the ground.
Fixing the table position at an unknown point by sighting two or three known points already plotted on the sheet.
A resection method that orients the table using two known points and an arbitrarily chosen auxiliary station.
A resection method that locates the table station from the angles subtended by three known points, solved graphically or by the trial-and-error method.
The ordered pair of northing and easting that fixes a point's position relative to a chosen origin.
The cross-product summation that gives the area of a closed polygon from the coordinates of its corners.
The station coordinates recomputed after traverse adjustment so that the figure closes exactly.
The direction of the gap between the start and the computed end, found from the total latitude and total departure errors.
The perimeter divided by the closing error, quoted as 1 in P/e and used to judge the quality of the work.
A local magnetic disturbance that deflects the compass needle away from the magnetic meridian.
A drawing board on a tripod, used with an alidade to plot survey lines directly in the field.
